## Submerged Aquatic Vegetation {#am_sav}

Trends in SAV percent cover were analyzed with a linear mixed effects
(LME) model of percent cover by year. The model treated the locations
sampled as a random effect to account for the fact that the locations
sampled in a managed area in any given year represent only a handful of
the many possible sampling locations. The same model was fit to each
taxonomic category in the data depending on the duration of the time
series and the performance of the model itself: species- or genus-level
analysis of turtle grass (Thalassia testudinum), shoal grass (Halodule
wrightii), widgeon grass (Ruppia maritima), manatee grass (Syringodium
filiforme), and Halophila species – stargrass (Halophila engelmannii);
paddle-grass (Halophila decipiens); and Johnson’s seagrass (Halophila
ovalis,
[formerly](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/southeast/endangered-species-conservation/frequently-asked-questions-removal-johnsons-seagrass)
Halophila johnsonii); analysis of macroalgae (categorized by whether the
algae had become detached and drifted into the monitoring site or was
growing attached to the substrate); all seagrasses considered together
(total seagrass), and/or all submerged aquatic vegetation (seagrass and
macroalgae) considered together (total SAV). The model was run only for
categories of SAV that were sampled during the growing season from April
to October and had at least five years of data. A result with a
significant, positive slope of the LME model indicates that percent
cover of a given species or group increased over time while a negative
slope indicates that it decreased.

Trends in water clarity were analyzed using records of chlorophyll a,
Secchi depth, and turbidity. A seasonal Kendall test to control the
effect of systematic differences in indicator values between months in
the trend analysis. For example, turbidity in the rainy season will
always tend to be higher than turbidity in the dry season. A significant
result for the seasonal Kendall test indicates a monotonically
increasing or decreasing trend across all seasons. The trend slope
estimate is called the Sen slope, or the Theil-Sen estimator, and is
calculated as the median of the slopes between all pairs of points
within each season. The Sen intercept was calculated as the median of
`y - mx` for all year-indicator value pairs in the time series, where
`y` is the indicator value, `m` is the Sen slope, and `x` is the year
corresponding with indicator value `y`.
